lectures.title: Overview: The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model

cues.en: In this lecture, I want to introduce you to the OSI model.
The OSI model or Open systems interconnection model is a model or a conceptual framework for understanding
and designing computer networks.
The purpose is that it's standardize the functions and protocol used in network communication.
It divides network communication into seven distinct layers, each with specific responsibilities.
This model was essential because in the 70s we had many different protocols and then it has been developed
and it has been released in the 80s.
And the idea here is that we do want competition between different protocols and between different companies.
But this competition should be interoperable in the sense that we can have one network with devices
of multiple vendors in them.
This is something that we nowadays take for granted.
We can just take our smartphone phone from whatever vendor it is and use it in pretty much every Wi-Fi
network.
And it doesn't really matter which vendor or which company has produced the Wi-Fi access point or which
company has produced the smartphone, it's interoperable.
And this is a little bit the idea behind all of those standards.
But there's also another idea that's more related to us here in this course.
By learning about the OSI model, we will be able to communicate more clearly about potential networking
problems.
So we could, for example, say we got a problem on the data link layer.
And the problem then is more clearly defined.
Here.
In this case, it would, for example, mean without spoiling too much now, but it would, for example,
mean that, yes, we do have a physical connection, but somehow we can't transmit anything over that
physical connection for whatever reason.
And by using this common language, we can communicate that way more clearly.
So it's essential that we have a look at the OSI model, because this will then also help us to understand
the networking stack and how all the networking works together.
So let's have a look at the OSI model.
I will be mentioning quite a few technical terms.
Now.
Those technical terms will become clearer during this chapter, and I am aware that you might not yet
be familiar with those.
But I know quite a few of my students will have worked with networks before and they will know some
of those terms.
So I feel kind of like obliged to mention those.
But if you don't recognize them or you don't know them yet, don't feel discouraged.
That's totally.
All right.
We'll all have a look at that later here in this chapter, we start here at the bottom, at the slide,
at the physical layer.
That's also the layer one or the so called layer one of the OSI model.
And it handles the transmission of raw data bits over a physical medium.
So for example, cable or switches.
So we got that one that is the lowest layer of our network communication.
Then on top of that, we got the data link layer that provides error free data transfer between adjacent
network nodes.
So for example, through Ethernet or Mac addresses, but it's not really routed to a destination.
So it's pretty much maybe your computer talking to another computer in the same network or your computer
talking to the router in your network.
But we can't do any hops on that layer.
So this is still really, really local.
Then we got a network layer on top.
This will allow us to make hops or manages data routing and forwarding between networks.
This will allow us, for example, if we are, let's say, in Europe and we want to communicate to a
server in Australia to just communicate to it without needing a dedicated connection there.
And this is really essential because pretty much we are not connected directly to pretty much anything
of the internet.
Everything goes through multiple hops or multiple routers to eventually reach the destination.
So this is really essential.
So this would now allow us, for example, that our we send a packet to our router and that one forwards
that to the internet and now we can access the internet and we can link networks together.
Then on top of those layers we got the transport layer.
This ensures reliable data transfer between hosts because packets might get lost on the way for certain
reasons.
We'll have a look at those later, but then we would, for example, need to retransmit those data or
maybe we don't want to retransmit those data.
And this has happening on the transport layer.
It just ensures that the data, for example, with TCP, that the data is ordered and that no data is
missing.
Meaning if data is missing, we will resend this data.
Then on top of that, we got a session layer.
It manages and controls the establishment maintenance and termination of sessions between applications.
Then on top of that, we got a presentation layer.
It translates, encrypts and compresses data for transmission between applications and the network.
So for example, that would be the SSL encryption of Https that everything is encrypted.
We can could consider that to be layer six.
And then on top of that one, we got the application layer.
This then provides the interface for applications to communicate over the network.
So that then would be, for example, Http, FTP, Smtp, SSH and so on.
So there we got our data layer.
Sometimes those layers are not that separate as they look here.
So sometimes, for example, we might not really use a session layer here or a certain protocol might
be considered to operate on two layers.
So stuff like this happens.
So this is more like a rough overview that gives us a general guidance of how our network can be structured.
We will have a look at each of those layers more in detail in this chapter, and we will work our way
up from the bottom to the top and examine each layer independently.
It's just important that you're aware of the grand scheme of things, how all of those layers work together,
because this will help you to understand what's important on each layer.
But this is the rough overview and we'll have a look at each of those layers later.
So the OSI model is interesting for us because it enables modularity.
